Let m = n+1 be positive. The map −/m : Cyc_0 → Set sends (X, t) to the quotient X/m (infinite_quotient_set). The map q : Cyc_0 → Cyc_m sends (X, t) to the cycle (X/m, t̄) with t̄[x] = [t x] (infinite_quotient_cycle, QuotientCycle, quotient_successor). This cycle lies in the component of the standard m-cycle (quotient_cycle_standard). The map r : Cyc_m → Set is the underlying set (cycle_component_set). The equation r∘q = −/m holds by refl (quotient_set_triangle). The map r has set fibers (cycle_component_set_covering). The map q has connected fibers, hence it is 0-connected (infinite_quotient_connected_fibers, infinite_quotient_zero_connected). The first proof of connectedness is different from the printed one. The printed proof identifies the fiber over the standard m-cycle with Cyc_0 through ρ_m. Instead, this proof compares identifications of cycles by evaluation at a merely chosen point. It uses the pointed identifications of lem:IdCycle. The next exercise carries out the printed route. The resulting factorization (infinite_quotient_factorization) is proved equal to the canonical 0-image factorization by thm:n-im-univ-prop (infinite_quotient_factorization_unique). No circle is involved. Module 285 also reproduces the printed step. Cyc_m is connected, and connectedness is a proposition. Thus the connectedness of q⁻¹(pt_m) from φ/ψ (quotient_fiber_connected) transports to every fiber. Hence q is 0-connected (quotient_zero_connected_from_standard). This gives the 0-image factorization by the printed route (infinite_quotient_factorization_via_standard_fiber).

The formalization completes the details of the printed proof of thm:image-Z-to-Cm for positive m = n+1, with the literal maps. The map φ : Cyc_0 → q⁻¹(pt_m) sends (X, t) to (ρ_m(X, t), e⁻¹) (quotient_fiber_phi). Here e : (Fin m × X)/m ≃ ℤ/m, [(k, x)] ↦ k, is induced by the residue of the root. This residue preserves the cycle structure. The resulting identification pt_m = q(ρ_m(X, t)) is e⁻¹. The standard m-cycle is the project's ℤ/m on remainders. The map ψ sends ((Y, u), e') to the class e'(0) of Y/m, taken as a set, with u^m restricted. The formalization shows that this is an infinite cycle, because its periods are zero (quotient_fiber_psi, class_cycle, class_cycle_infinite). The proof of ψ∘φ = id uses two facts. The class e⁻¹(0) consists exactly of the pairs (0, x). Also, x ↦ (0, x) is an isomorphism of cycles (quotient_fiber_psi_phi). The proof of φ∘ψ = id shows that (k, v) ↦ u^k(v) is an isomorphism of cycles Fin m × V ≅ Y (quotient_fiber_phi_psi). It compares the second components by evaluation at 0. Hence φ is an equivalence Cyc_0 ≃ q⁻¹(pt_m) with inverse ψ (quotient_fiber_equiv). As the printed proof concludes, the fiber is connected (quotient_fiber_connected). The 0-connectedness of q in thm:image-Z-to-Cm is proved independently and does not use this result.

Let d be an order and m = n+1 positive. Then md is read as the order of the root (order_root), with period subgroup m·H_d. The notation "md" is literal only for principal d. The map ρ_m restricts to Cyc_d → Cyc_md (cycle_root_of_order). Every fiber of this restriction is equivalent to X/m (root_order_fiber_equiv, root_order_fiber_set). The proof uses thm:fiber-cdg and the cancellation of m in period subgroups. Thus −/m is literally the family of fibers of ρ_m (root_order_fibers). It lifts to q : Cyc_md → Cyc_m, (X, t) ↦ (X/m, t̄) (order_quotient_cycle). Here r : Cyc_m → Set is the underlying set. The triangle is a proved identification of families (root_order_fiber_triangle). The result is a 0-image factorization (root_fibers_factorization). More generally, −/m on Cyc_e factors this way for every order e divisible by m (order_quotient_factorization). A chain of equivalences identifies the preimage of q at the standard m-cycle with Cyc_d (root_quotient_preimage_equiv). Identifications (ℤ/m, s) = (X/m, t̄) correspond to maps of cycles X → ℤ/m. These maps correspond to classes in X/m (order_quotient_preimage_classes). These classes correspond to fibers of ρ_m. The sum of the fibers is Cyc_d.

Let n = b+1 > 0 and let A be a groupoid. Consider the map ev_{n,A}(f) = (f(pt_n), ap_f(σ_n), !). It goes from Cyc_n (CycleComponent (b+1)) → A to Σ(a : A) Σ(s : a = a) (refl a = sⁿ). This map is a BookIsEquiv (cyc_evaluation_is_equiv). The BookEquiv with map cyc_evaluation is cyc_universal_property. Here σ_n is literally the symmetry (s⁻¹, !) whose permutation is the modular predecessor (cyc_generator, standard_predecessor_loop). The formalization proves refl = σ_nⁿ in pt_n = pt_n (cyc_generator_order). The power sⁿ is loop_power_nat, with the book's orientation refl a = sⁿ. T(x) is the book's type, with the condition π(τσ_n) = π(τ)s (CycLiftData). T(pt_n) is contractible (cyc_lift_base_contractible). The reason is that the loops at pt_n under σ_n-composition form a cycle. Also, maps of cycles into (a = b, s·) are determined by their value at refl. Connectedness gives T(x) for all x (cyc_lift_contractible). Unlike the book, the formalization replaces the proposition part (U, V, χ) by a quasi-inverse. The law ev∘g = id uses the naturality of the lifts, which is proved by path induction (cyc_lift_naturality, cyc_lift_coherence). The formalization proves the formal parts of the corollary after the proof. Families of sets over Cyc_n are equivalent to sets with a permutation t such that tⁿ = id. This equivalence uses transport along ap_S(σ_n) (cyc_set_families_permutations). The total space is connected iff this monodromy is cyclic (cyc_family_connected_cyclic). Hence connected set families over Cyc_n are equivalent to the cycles with tⁿ = id (cyc_connected_set_families). Also, tⁿ = id is equivalent to "the order divides n" (cycle_period_order_divides). Module 285 formalizes the sentence about decidable coverings. Families S : Cyc_n → Set of decidable sets with connected total space are equivalent to decidable cycles with t^n = id. By connectedness, decidability at all points is the same as decidability at pt_n. Such cycles are finite, because decidability gives a least positive period. Without LPO, they are equivalent to Σ_m ((m+1) | n) × Component(Z/(m+1), s) (cyc_decidable_connected_coverings_classification). These are the usual finite cycles of order dividing n.

Let (X, t) and (Y, u) be cycles and x₀ : X. A map of cycles is an f with uf = ft pointwise. The type of maps of cycles is equivalent to P × Y through f ↦ (!, f(x₀)) (cycle_map_point_equiv). Here P = ord(u) | ord(t), that is, H_t ⊆ H_u. The formalization proves the following remark: ord(u) | ord(t) iff there merely is a map of cycles (X, t) → (Y, u) (cycle_map_divides, divides_cycle_map). This block is in a draft (wip) section of the book.

(Order, |) is a partial order on a set (order_set, order_divides_refl, order_divides_trans, order_divides_antisym). It has binary meets and joins. The meet has period subgroup H_d + H_k, and the join has H_d ∩ H_k (order_meet, order_join, SubgroupSum, SubgroupIntersection). The formalization also proves their universal properties (order_meet_divides_left, order_meet_divides_right, order_meet_greatest, order_join_divided_left, order_join_divided_right, order_join_least). The finite order 1 is least (one_divides), and the infinite order is greatest (divides_infinite). The words "gcd" and "lcm" are literal only for principal orders, where 0 is the infinite order. For these orders, the meet and join are the principal orders of the numerical gcd and lcm (principal_meet_gcd, principal_join_lcm). Euclid's algorithm computes gcd, with aℤ + bℤ = gcd(a, b)ℤ (nat_gcd, nat_gcd_sum). The lcm is the least positive common multiple, or 0 if a factor is 0. It satisfies aℤ ∩ bℤ = lcm(a, b)ℤ (nat_lcm, nat_lcm_intersection). The formalization proves that both are the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple for the divisibility of natural numbers. This theorem is in a draft (wip) section of the book.

The statements hold for every circle C (CircleSignature). The map n ↦ loopⁿ is an equivalence ℤ ≃ (base = base) (circle_group_usym_integers, cor:S1groupoid). Every symmetry is loop^{wind(g)} (circle_every_symmetry_power). Composition corresponds to addition: loopⁿ · loopᵐ = loop^{n+m} in the book's order (circle_power_mul). In concatenation order, this is circle_power_concat. The winding number changes · into + (circle_winding_mul). The sentence that the circle 'efficiently packages' the group of integers is motivational.

The pointed type (FinSet_2, 2) is BΣ_2 by definition (finset_two_pointed, refl). Its symmetries 2 = 2 are identifications in FinSet_2 = Set_(Fin 2). These symmetries are exactly refl and swap. Evaluation at 0 gives USym Σ_2 ≃ Fin 2 (sigma2_usym_equiv). Every symmetry is refl or swap (sigma2_cases). Also, swap ≠ refl and swap · swap = refl. The exercise xca:C2 itself is about Bool = Bool in U (bool_loops_equiv, ch2). The formalization proves it again here for Fin 2 in FinSet_2. For every circle C, the map S¹ → FinSet_2 with base ↦ 2 and loop ↦ swap is circle recursion. Its computation rule is an identification (circle_finset_two_beta). As a pointed map, it sends loop to swap (circle_finset_two_loop). The sentence 'We saw this already in fig:covering' is a cross-reference.

Footnote: the formal statement gives the ternary operation (p, q, r) ↦ p q⁻¹ r on a = a'. It uses the book composition order, that is, concat (concat r q⁻¹) p. It gives the heap laws p p⁻¹ r = r and p r⁻¹ r = p. The heap axioms proper are in sec:heaps. Transport along f : a = a' in x ↦ (a = x) is the equivalence l ↦ l · f from a = a to a = a'. This equivalence is judgmentally concat, and it respects the ternary operation. Some statements are informal: a = a' has no obvious binary composition and no distinguished element. The affine-plane analogy is also informal. These statements make no mathematical claim beyond the above.

By lem:subtype-eq-= (component_path_equiv), the first projection A_(a) → A induces an equivalence ((a,!) = (a,!)) ≃ (a = a). The underlying map of this equivalence is ap_fst, by refl (component_loops_equiv_map). A_(a) is connected (native_component_connected). The conclusions ('we should consider only connected types', 'only groupoids') are motivation for def:pt-conn-groupoid.

U^{=1}_* is the core record PointedConnectedGroupoid (carrier, point, connected, groupoid). The literal Σ(A : U)(A × isconn(A) × isgrpd(A)) is PointedConnectedGroupoidSigma. The two types are equivalent, and both round trips hold by refl. Margin note: U^{≤1} = Groupoid = Σ A isgrpd(A) is GroupoidTypes, and U^{≤1}_* is PointedGroupoids (module 284). U^{>0} = Σ A isconn(A) is ConnectedTypes, and U^{>0}_* is PointedConnectedType (module 485). U is Narya's Type.

Refuted: part 2 as printed ('A is a groupoid iff a = a is a set', for arbitrary A) is false. For A = U and a = ∅, the loop type is a set, but U is not a groupoid. This is defgroup_unconditional_fails (module 411), which uses universe_not_groupoid of module 487. In general, only 'A groupoid ⇒ a = a set' holds (groupoid_loops_set). Corrected statement: part 2 holds under Π(x:A) ‖a = x‖ (based_groupoid_loops_equiv), that is, for connected A (connected_groupoid_loops_equiv). The conclusion uses it in this form. Part 1, Connected A ≃ Π(x:A) ‖a = x‖ (connected_based_equiv), is proved as printed. The conclusion U^{=1}_* ≃ Σ(A:U) Σ(a:A) ((Π_x ‖a = x‖) × isSet(a = a)) (pcg_defgroup_equiv) is also proved as printed. Blind statement check: our statement refutes the blind literal statement, and the blind corrected variant is our statement (bridged-corrected).

(A, a) determines (A, a, p, q). Any two connectedness and groupoid witnesses give equal elements of U^{=1}_* (pcg_witnesses_unique). The reason is that isconn(A) and isgrpd(A) are propositions (connected_prop, isgroupoid_isprop). Paths in U^{=1}_* are paths of pointed types (pcg_path_pointed_equiv, core). The naming convention itself is informal.

Group is a one-field record (classifying : U^{=1}_*) with the constructor mkgroup. The book uses the data type Copy of sec:unary-sum-types (module 16) instead. Records have judgmental eta. Thus mkgroup(B G) ≡ G and B(mkgroup X) ≡ X hold by refl (group_eta, group_beta). Also, identifications of groups compute fieldwise. The footnote on the name mkgroup is informal.
B : Group → U^{=1}_* is the record projection group_B. BG G is the pointed type (A, a). The designated shape sh_G = pt_BG is shape G. The typographical footnote is informal.
Ω X ≔ (pt_X = pt_X), pointed at refl, is Omega X (core). Its underlying type is Loop X of module 00.
USym G ≔ Ω BG is a set (usym_set). Footnote: USym : Group → Set is usym_set_type, and USym(mkgroup X) ≡ ΩX (usym_mkgroup, refl). The 'symmetries in / of' remark is terminology.

The core defines IsFiniteGroup G ≔ IsFinite (USym G) and Card(G) ≔ Card(USym G). Litmus tests: Card(C_m) = m (cyclic_group_fin_card), Card(Σ_2) = 2 (sigma2_card) and Card(Σ_n) = n! (symmetric_group_card).

The constructor and the destructor give Group ≃ U^{=1}_* (group_classifying_equiv). U^{=1}_* is the subtype of U_* given by the proposition 'connected groupoid' (pcg_pointed_subtype_equiv, pcg_structure_prop). A pointed connected groupoid X is B(mkgroup X) by refl (group_beta). There is an equivalence (G = H) ≃ (BG = BH), with BG and BH as pointed types (group_path_pointed_equiv). This equivalence sends refl to refl (group_path_pointed_refl).

Group is a one-field record with judgmental eta. Thus a definition of f(G) for G ≡ mkgroup X is literally a definition on G .classifying. No induction principle of Copy is necessary (group_eta is refl). The footnote about notation is informal.
For a groupoid A, Aut_A(a) ≔ mkgroup(A_(a), (a, !)). The groupoid witness is an explicit argument hA. By definition, BAut_A(a) ≡ (A_(a), (a,!)).

For connected A, fst : A_(a) → A is a BookIsEquiv, because its fibers ‖a = x‖ are inhabited propositions. It is also a pointed equivalence, pointed by refl a. Hence mkgroup(A, a) = Aut_A(a) (pcg_automorphism_path, through group_path_from_pointed_equiv). Also, G = Aut_BG(sh_G) for every group G (group_shape_automorphism_path).

The statements hold for every circle C. Z ≔ mkgroup(S¹, base) is circle_group C, with BZ ≡ (S¹, base) (refl). S¹ is a connected groupoid. There is an equivalence base = base ≃ ℤ, with composition as addition (module 413). Z = Aut_S¹(base) (circle_group_automorphism_path). At the constructed circle, this is integer_group (module 405). InfCyc = Σ(X:U) Σ(t:X → X) ‖(ℤ, s) = (X, t)‖ is InfiniteCycles up to reassociation of Σ (infinite_cycles_book_form_equiv, refl round trips). S¹ ≃ InfCyc is thm:S1bysymmetries (circle_infinite_cycles_equiv).

There are two identifications Z = Aut_Cyc(ℤ, s) (= cyclic_group 0). The constructed circle of chapter 3 is S¹ ≔ Cyc_0, based at (ℤ, s). Thus cyclic_group 0 is mkgroup of the same pointed type with its own witnesses (circle_group_with). The identity and the flip of the circle give two pointed equivalences BZ ≃ BAut_Cyc(ℤ, s). The flip is rem:flipthecircle: base ↦ base, loop ↦ loop⁻¹, an equivalence by circle_reflection_equiv. The two identifications differ (integer_cyclic_paths_differ). The isomorphism recovered from a path of groups sends loop to loop or to loop⁻¹, respectively. The winding numbers of these loops are 1 and −1. Module 413 proves this for every circle (circle_group_paths_differ).

(1) TG = Aut_Prop(true), with true = true contractible. TG is identified with Aut_Prop(P) for every proposition P and with mkgroup(true, triv) (unit_group). It is also identified with mkgroup(C, c) for contractible C and with Aut_S(x) for every set S. All of these use 'symmetries contractible ⇒ trivial' (usym_contractible_trivial). (2) Σ_n = Aut_Set(Fin n), with BΣ_n ≡ (FinSet_n, n) by refl. Here FinSet_n is the groupoid of n-element sets (book_finite_sets_at_equiv). Also, Σ_n = Aut_FinSet(n), Σ_n = Aut_{FinSet_n}(n) and Σ_n = Aut_U(n), where U_(n) is a groupoid (universe_set_automorphism_group, module 485). (3) Σ_S = Aut_Set(S), with BΣ_S ≡ (Set_(S), S). Set is not connected (set_types_not_connected). Footnote: module 421 uses universes as smallness predicates of modules 190-193. Prop_U : U' and true : Prop_U. Group_U ≃ Copy(U^{=1}_*) lies in U' (group_in_upper). Aut_{Prop_U}(true) is trivial, with classifying type in U'. Aut_true(triv) is in Group_U for every U. With the hypothesis Replacement U, Σ_S ∈ Group_U for S : Set_U, and Aut_Group(G) ∈ Group_U for G ∈ Group_U. The final sentence (some groups lie only in higher Group_i) is not formalizable here.

Aut_Prop(P) = TG for every proposition P, because PropTypes is a set. Σ_S is trivial when S is a proposition, because S ≃ S is then contractible. Thus Σ_0, Σ_1 and Σ_false are trivial. Here Σ_0 = Σ_∅ by definition (Fin 0 ≡ ∅), and false = ∅. Aut_FinSet(n) = Σ_n through the subtype FinSet ⊆ Set (automorphism_group_subtype_path with component_subtype_equiv). Aut_Set(ℕ) = Aut_Set(ℤ) follows from the equivalence ℕ ≃ ℤ of module 288, a parity encoding (module 415).

C_m ≔ Aut_Cyc(m, s) is cyclic_group_fin n, with m = n+1 and the literal (Fin m, s). It is identified with cyclic_group m on (ℤ/m, s). The image of 0 gives a correspondence between the m symmetries and 0, …, m−1 (cyclic_group_fin_usym_equiv). On ℤ/m, this is cyclic_group_eval_equiv. Composition corresponds to addition mod m, a ⊕ b ≔ s^b(a), with 0 as the unit (cyclic_group_eval_mul, eval_unit). Every symmetry is a power of the generator (cycle_group_symmetries_are_powers). Footnote: C_1 = TG. C_2 = Σ_2, with exactly one nontrivial symmetry f, and f² = id. Σ_m has m! symmetries. A count shows C_3 ≠ Σ_3. The chain C_m = Aut_{Σ(X:Set)(X ≃ X)}(m, s) = Aut_{SetBundle(S¹)}(S¹, dg_m) = Aut_{S¹→Set}(R_m) =: ℤ/mℤ is proved for every circle (cyclic_integers_mod_path). The proof uses thm:coveringsofS1perms. In the first step, the book writes Σ(X:Set)(X → X), but the theorem uses X ≃ X. We also use X ≃ X.

The statements hold for every circle C and m = n+1. The map prj : Cyc_m → FinSet_m, ((X,t),!) ↦ (X,!), pointed by refl, is the forgetful homomorphism C_m → Σ_m. Its fiber at X is Σ(t : X ≃ X) ‖(m, s) = (X, t)‖, a set (cycle_forget_fiber_equiv). This fiber uses permutations, not endomaps t : X → X, in agreement with def:Cyc. R_m : BZ → BΣ_m is the circle recursion base ↦ m, loop ↦ s. Its computation rule gives its pointing (book: R_m(base) ≡ m). Its underlying set family is ch3's R_m (power_finset_underlying). C'_m ≔ mkgroup(Σ_{X:FinSet_m} ‖R_m⁻¹(X)‖_0, (m, |(base, β)|_0)) is the 0-image group (cyclic_image_group). Here β is the pointing of R_m, not refl. As pointed maps, R_m = prj ∘ mod_m. Also, mod_m is 0-connected, because all symmetries of C_m are powers of the generator. Thus ‖R_m⁻¹(X)‖_0 ≃ prj⁻¹(X) = cycle structures on X (power_fiber_cycle_structures). Also, BC'_m ≃ BC_m as pointed types, and this gives C'_m = C_m (cyclic_image_path). The book factors through c : S¹ ≃ Cyc_0 and −/m of thm:image-Z-to-Cm. Instead, we factor through mod_m directly. Uniqueness is zero_image_universal_property. The roots-of-unity picture (fig:m-cycle-roots) and the footnote on quotient groups and images are informal or forward references.

For every circle C, ‖R_2⁻¹(2)‖_0 is contractible (rm_two_fiber_contractible). It is the set of cycle structures on 2, and the only cyclic permutation of Fin 2 is the swap (fin2_cyclic_is_swap). Every 2-element set has exactly one cycle structure. Thus prj : Cyc_2 → FinSet_2 is an equivalence, and C_2 = Σ_2 (cyclic_two_symmetric_two_path). The exercise says that the contractibility reflects this identification. The footnote (C_2 = Σ_2 is contractible) refers to a later chapter.

The symmetries of sh_{C'_m} in BC'_m are equivalent to the subgroup generated by s = R_m(loop): USym(C'_m) ≃ Σ(σ : m = m) ‖Σ(k : ℤ) sᵏ = σ‖ (cyclic_image_symmetries). The equivalence is the composite of transport along C'_m = C_m and σ ↦ Ω(prj)(σ). The second map is injective, because its permutation determines a cycle automorphism. Its image is exactly the set of powers of s. The formalization does not prove that the equivalence is literally Ω of the inclusion BC'_m → BΣ_m. It is the explicit composite above.

G × H ≔ mkgroup(BG × BH), pointed at (sh_G, sh_H) (core). The lemma product_group_classifying holds by refl. USym(G × H) ≃ USym G × USym H, with componentwise composition. The Klein four-group Σ_2 × Σ_2 has four symmetries (klein_card).

C_4 = Σ_2 × Σ_2 is impossible (klein_not_cyclic). Every symmetry of the Klein group squares to the identity (klein_exponent_two). Identifications of groups transport this property. But the generator of C_4 on ℤ/4 squares to 2 ≠ 0 (computed by refl). C_4 is the literal cyclic_group_fin 3, identified with cyclic_group 4 by cyclic_group_fin_path.

Core (module 407): let S be finite (IsFinite S, that is, merely an n-element set), and let G : S → Group. Then Π_s G(s) ≔ mkgroup(Π_s BG(s), s ↦ sh_{G(s)}). By function extensionality, ptw (happly) gives USym(Π_s G(s)) ≃ Π_s USym G(s).

(i) A finite product of connected types is connected (connected_pi_finite, core, by finite choice). Products of groupoids are groupoids. (ii) For S = Bool, the product of a family equals the binary product G(false) × G(true). The pointed equivalence f ↦ (f(false), f(true)) gives this identification (bool_family_product_path). Footnote: for an arbitrary family, the component of s ↦ sh_{G(s)} is a group (component_product_group), with USym ≃ Π_s USym G(s). For finite S, this group is equal to the product. The Axiom-of-Choice alternative is not formalized.

Forward references: lem:idtypesgiveabstractgroups (usym_abstract_laws, module 403) gives the group laws. The characterization by these laws (lem:Groupsareidentitytypes) belongs to chapter 7. It is not formalized here.

The core defines isAb(G) ≔ Π(g, h : USym G) gh = hg, with gh = usym_mul G g h. This is a proposition. The core also defines AbGroup ≔ Σ(G : Group) isAb(G). The preceding prose (Z abelian) is circle_group_is_abelian.
Σ_2 is abelian, because its two automorphisms of Fin 2 commute. Σ_3 is not abelian: (1 2)(0 1) and (0 1)(1 2) differ at 0 (module 406). The product of abelian groups is abelian (componentwise).

The one-point union X ∨ Y is OnePointUnionSignature X Y. This is a type with inl, inr, glue and dependent induction, and its computation rule is an identification. Narya has no HITs. Thus every result holds for every inhabitant, and the formalization constructs none. Let W be any wedge of BG with itself. Take fold (the identity on both summands) and the inclusion (inl x ↦ (x, sh), inr x ↦ (sh, x)), pointed by their computation rules. Then the type of pointed factorizations Σ(h : BG × BG →* BG)(h ∘ incl = fold) is a proposition (wedge_factorization_prop). It is equivalent to isAb(G) (wedge_factorization_abelian_equiv). The first sentences say that classifying types of abelian groups are identity types of 2-types. They refer to sec:abelian-groups and are not formalized here.
Take mkgroup(A, a), with its connectedness and groupoid witnesses, and any b : A. Then ‖mkgroup(A, a) = mkgroup(A, b)‖, by connectedness. The same holds for ∞-groups (module 485).

Core (module 402): G = H is a set, and Group is a groupoid. Aut(G) ≔ Aut_Group(G) (group_aut). Its symmetries are the identifications G = G, or equivalently the isomorphisms G → G (group_aut_usym_isos).

AbstractGroup is the record (carrier, unit, mul, inv, laws), with laws : AbstractGroupLaws carrier unit mul inv. The book's g1·g2 is mul g1 g2. The only deviation is in the packaging. The laws are grouped as GroupLaws of absgroup.tex. The field carrier_set gives isSet(S) (the book's 'a set S'). The unit law (a) is split into unit_right (g·e = g) and unit_left (e·g = g). Associativity and the law of inverses (g·g⁻¹ = e) are as printed.

The equations are propositions: AbstractGroupLaws S e mul inv is a proposition (abstract_group_laws_prop). Two abstract groups with the same data and different proofs of the laws are equal (abstract_group_laws_irrelevant). The subtype convention itself is notation.

Let G be a group. Take USym G with e = refl, g⁻¹ = inverse g and h·g = trans(g)(h) = concat g h (usym_mul G h g). Then USym G satisfies the laws. USym G is a set, because BG is a groupoid (usym_set). The laws come from xca:path-groupoid-laws. The book's judgmental e·g ≡ g is the identification concat_p1, because Narya's J has a typal β-rule. The lemma loop_space_group_laws states the same for any loop space a = a that is a set. The lemma abstr_is_loop_space_group checks by refl that abstr G is its instance at sh_G.
abstr G is the abstract group (USym G, refl, usym_mul G, usym_inv G, usym_abstract_laws G).

X → S with the pointwise operations is an abstract group (abstract_group_of_maps, for a set X). The set hypothesis on X is not necessary: pointwise_abstract_group works for any type. The neutral element is x ↦ e, and the product is pointwise judgmentally (litmus refl). The claim 'Abelian iff G is' is false as printed. G abelian ⇒ X → S abelian holds for every X (pointwise_abelian). The converse holds when X is merely inhabited (pointwise_abelian_reflect, abstract_group_of_maps_abelian_iff). For X = ∅, the group of maps is abelian, but abstr(Σ_3) is not (abstract_group_of_maps_abelian_converse_fails).

The book says 'without loss of generality pt_BH ≡ k(pt_BG) and k_pt ≡ refl'. The formalization realizes this with H := mkgroup(B, k(sh_G)) for a connected groupoid B and k : BG÷ → B. Then sh_H ≡ k(sh_G) judgmentally (homom_eqs_shape). The map f := ap_k : USym G → USym H satisfies f(refl) ≡ refl (refl, 'true by definition' as printed). By lem:apcomp, it also satisfies f(g⁻¹) = f(g)⁻¹ and f(g'·g) = f(g')·f(g). That is, f is an abstract homomorphism (homom_eqs_abstract_hom). The lemma homom_eqs_usym_hom identifies USym of (k, refl) with ap_k (rem:loops-map). The reduction of the general case is lem:grouphomomaxioms.

Hom(G,H) is GroupHom G H, with the constructor mkhom and the destructor hom_B (classifying map Bf). Here hom_function = Bf÷ and hom_point = Bf_pt : sh_H = Bf÷(sh_G), in the book orientation. Deviation: the formalization uses a one-field record with judgmental eta instead of the data type Copy_mkgroup. Thus mkhom and B are mutually inverse judgmentally (group_hom_classifying_equiv). So the Copy induction principle is trivial. The footnote 'we may write f : G → H' is notation.

loops_map X Y k p = concat k_pt (concat (ap_k p) k_pt⁻¹). This is the book's k_pt⁻¹ · ap_{k÷}(p) · k_pt in concatenation order (k_pt first). The pointing path (Ωk)_pt has type refl = Ωk(refl) (loops_map_point, by the inverse law). In the book, Ωk(refl) ≡ k_pt⁻¹·k_pt judgmentally. Here, Ωk(refl) = concat k_pt (concat refl k_pt⁻¹), and the unit law is part of the proved identification.

For k = (f, refl_{f x}), Ωk = ap_f as functions (x = x) → (f x = f x). The proof uses funext and the identification loop_conjugate_at_refl. This identification is not judgmental, because concat refl p ≡ p fails in HOTT.
usym_hom G H f := loops_map (BG G) (BG H) (hom_B G H f). This is literally Ω Bf.

The formalization proves the three identities with the printed orientations. They are USym f(refl) = refl, USym f(g⁻¹) = (USym f(g))⁻¹ and USym f(g'·g) = USym f(g')·USym f(g) (usym_mul notation). As in the book's proof, path induction eliminates the pointing path (inside loop_conjugate_inverse/concat). This reduces the identities to lem:apcomp. In the source, the labels gp-homo-comp/gp-homo-inv are attached to the inverse/product lines in swapped order. The formalization covers both.

f is an isomorphism iff Bf÷ is a (book) equivalence. Iso(G,H) = Σ(f : Hom(G,H)) IsGroupIso f is a subset, because IsGroupIso is a proposition. The footnote (both are sets) is group_hom_set and group_iso_set.
id_G := mkhom(id_BG), with id_BG = (identity, refl) of def:pointedidentity. It is an isomorphism (group_hom_id_iso). The lemma usym_hom_id shows that USym(id_G) is the identity (an identification).

(G = H) ≃ Iso(G,H). This equivalence is composed from the record eta of Group and the subtype U^{=1}_* ⊆ U_*. The other parts are xca:pointedequiv (pointed_path_equiv) and BookPointedEquiv(BG,BH) ≃ Iso(G,H). The convention to write p : Iso(G,H) for p : G = H (and Bp for the pointed equivalence) is notation. The formalization always applies group_path_iso_equiv / group_path_from_iso explicitly.

group_hom_compose G G' G'' f f' = mkhom(Bf' ∘ Bf) is the book's f' ∘ f, with book_pointed_compose of def:pointedtypes. The argument order is first f, then f'. The formalization adds unit and associativity laws.

To define φ : Π(f : Hom(G,H)) T(f), it is sufficient to give φ(mkhom k) for all pointed maps k. This is group_hom_induction (by record eta). Its computation rule is judgmental (group_hom_induction_beta is refl). The footnote is notation.

Hom(G,H) is a set, by the book's argument. Identifications of homomorphisms are pairs (h, h(sh_G)·Bf_pt = Bf'_pt). With h : Bf÷ = Bf'÷ as printed, this is group_hom_path_data_equiv. With homotopies, it is group_hom_path_equiv. Two such h agree at sh_G by cancellation of Bf_pt. Hence they agree everywhere by connectedness (pointed_homotopy_prop). Footnote ft:ptd-decr-h-lev: the first sentence is pointed_maps_set. The general claim is pointed_maps_truncation_level_book: if X is (k−1)-connected, Y is (n+k)-truncated, k ≥ 0 and n ≥ −1, then X →* Y is an n-type. It is proved for all n ≥ −2 through pointed sections (pointed_sections_hlevel) and HoTT Lemma 7.5.7 (module 285).

(1) The maps X ↦ X ⊔ T and X ↦ X × T on Set_(S), pointed by refl judgmentally, give Σ_S → Σ_{S⊔T} and Σ_S → Σ_{S×T}. For X ⊔ T, the image of g acts as g on S and as the identity on T. For X × T, it acts as g on the first components only. Σ_m → Σ_{m+n} and Σ_m → Σ_{mn} compose these maps with an isomorphism. This isomorphism comes from Fin(m+n) = Fin m ⊔ Fin n or from Fin(mn) = Fin m × Fin n (module 35). Its classifying map is X ↦ X, pointed by the identification, and it acts by conjugation. The product identification enumerates (a,b) as a + m·b. That is, the order is lexicographic, and the second component leads (the book leaves the choice open). Litmus: Σ_2 → Σ_3 sends the transposition to σ = (1 2), and Σ_2 → Σ_4 sends it to (0 1)(2 3). (2) Hom(G,1) and Hom(1,G) are contractible, with the book's homomorphisms as centers. This holds for 1 = unit_group, for the book's TG = Aut_Prop(true) and for mkgroup(bn 1, 0). The second statement uses contractible_domain_pointed_maps (lem:contract-away/lem:univ-cover-of-groupoid argument). (3) Module 404 gives the projections and inclusions. Their USym are projection and inclusion (litmus). (4) The statements hold for every circle C and m = n+1. R_m classifies a homomorphism Z → Σ_m (power_finset_hom). Its computation rule gives its pointing, but the book uses refl_m. The homomorphism mod_m : Z → C_m is classified by circle recursion base ↦ (m, s), loop ↦ s (the generating symmetry). Its computation rule gives its pointing, not reflexivity (mod_hom, mod_hom_loop). As homomorphisms, R_m = prj ∘ mod_m (mod_forget_hom_factorization). Here prj : C_m → Σ_m forgets the cycle structure (cyclic_forget_hom, pointed by refl). The isomorphism C_m ≅ ℤ/mℤ of ex:cyclicgroups is cyclic_integers_mod_path. This is an identification, and thus an isomorphism through group_path_iso_equiv.

Convention: a map f : A → B of groupoids induces Aut_A(a) → Aut_B(f a) (automorphism_group_map_hom). This homomorphism is classified by f on components and pointed by refl judgmentally. It acts by ap_f. The connectedness of A and B is not necessary. The example: τ̃ = (id, τ) with τ = (0 1). Then Ω(τ̃)(g) ≡ τ⁻¹·g·τ judgmentally (sigma3_tilde_tau_usym). If id_{Σ3} = τ̃, then τ commutes with every symmetry (sigma3_tilde_tau_commutes). This fails for σ = (1 2), because στ(0) = 2 and τσ(0) = 1 (module 406). Thus id_{Σ3} ≠ τ̃ (sigma3_two_homs_differ). The convention sentences about the omission of refl are notation.

Ω(g ∘ f) = Ωg ∘ Ωf as functions Ω X → Ω Z (funext of the pointwise version). As in the book, the proof uses induction on the pointing path of f and on a based path. The base case ap_{g∘f}(refl) ≡ ap_g(ap_f(refl)) ≡ refl is judgmental, as printed. But the proof also uses the unit laws of concat to remove the reflexive pointing paths, and these laws are identifications.
USym(ψ ∘ φ) = USym ψ ∘ USym φ as functions. This is the instance of def:loops-compose at Bφ and Bψ.

The statements hold for an arbitrary circle C, with Z = circle_group C. The group integer_group is the instance C = constructed_circle. ev_BG : ((S¹,base) →* BG) ≃ USym G is cor:circle-loopspace (module 129). Its map is literally (f÷, f_pt) ↦ Ω(f÷, f_pt)(loop) (refl). Both sides are sets. Hom(Z,G) ≃ USym G sends f to USym f(loop) judgmentally. The inverse ve(g) is circle recursion on (sh_G, g). In the book, ve(g)(base) ≡ sh_G judgmentally, and the pointing path is refl. Here, these become the base identification of the circle signature and its inverse (circle_hom_ve_base, circle_hom_ve_point). Also, ve(g)(loop) = g holds over that identification (circle_hom_ve_loop_over). It also holds as Ω(ve g)(loop) = g. Litmus: ev(id_Z) = loop and ev(trivial) = e.

ev_H(f ∘ k) = USym f(ev_G(k)) for all k : Hom(Z,G). This holds pointwise and as an identification of functions Hom(Z,G) → USym H. As in the book, the proof uses cor:USym-compose. Here f ∘ k is group_hom_compose Z G H k f.

For a group G and a groupoid A, the four types are equivalent. (2) and (3) are judgmentally the same, because BookPointedMap is that Σ-type. The equivalence (2)/(3) ≃ (1) is xca:freemaps. The equivalence (3) ≃ (4) is fiberwise. It uses that pointed maps from the connected BG into (A,a) are pointed maps into the component A_(a) (pointed_maps_into_component). This is the content of xca:ptd-conn-to-comp of actions.tex, and the formalization proves it here. It also uses Hom(G, Aut_A(a)) ≃ BG →* (A_(a), (a,!)). Litmus: a map f goes judgmentally to (f(sh_G), the homomorphism classified by f on components).

USym f(e_G) = e_H, USym f(g ·_G g') = USym f(g) ·_H USym f(g') and USym f(g⁻¹) = (USym f(g))⁻¹. These equations use the operations of abstr(G) and abstr(H) (usym_hom_abstract_equations). The definition abstr_hom packages USym f as an abstract homomorphism, that is, a multiplication-preserving map, as in absgroup.tex.

For p : sh_G = y, (id_BG, p⁻¹) : BG ≃* (BG÷, y) is a pointed equivalence. It gives the isomorphism conj_iso : G ≅ mkgroup(BG÷, y) and the identification conj_group_path. USym(mkgroup(BG÷,y)) ≡ (y = y) judgmentally (footnote). In the book's notation, Ω(id, p⁻¹)(g) = p g p⁻¹ (loop_conjugate). In concatenation order, this is p⁻¹, then g, then p. The proof uses inverse_inverse instead of the book's path induction. The map is transport in z ↦ (z = z) along p. Hence it is an equivalence (sh_G = sh_G) ≃ (y = y). Litmus: for y = sh_G, conjugation is g ↦ p·g·p⁻¹ in usym_mul notation (judgmental). Conjugation is trivial in abelian groups, and conjugation by τ moves σ in Σ_3.

inn : Hom(G, Aut(G)) has Binn(y) = (mkgroup(BG÷, y), w_y) in the component of Group at G. Here w_y : ‖G = mkgroup(BG÷, y)‖ comes from the connectedness of BG and conj_group_path ('the codomain of Binn is correct'). Binn(sh_G) ≡ G judgmentally (record eta). The book's p_inn := refl_G is the component path whose first component is refl_G judgmentally (inn_point_fst). The reason is that the truncation components differ as terms of a proposition. Litmus: as an identification G = G, USym(inn)(g) is ap_{y ↦ mkgroup(BG÷,y)}(g) (inn_usym_fst). Its shape component is g (judgmentally). Transport of a symmetry h along it gives g·h·g⁻¹ (inn_usym_acts_by_conjugation). Hence inn acts trivially for abelian G, and USym(inn)(τ) ≠ e in Σ_3 (inn_sigma3_tau_nontrivial).

ParityRelated E hE P f g says that the subset {e | f e ≠ g e} (ParityDisagreement) has an even number of elements. This subset is finite, because two-element sets have decidable equality (parity_disagreement_finite). Here IsEvenNat n ≔ Σ k, n = k + k. This is equivalent to nat_odd n = false (is_even_nat_iff). The finite set E has an explicit IsFinite witness hE. The family P lands in BΣ_2 = BookFiniteSetsAt 2. The footnote's decidability of the parity relation is parity_related_decidable.

The relation ∼ is an EquivalenceRelation (parity_relation). The quotient is the set quotient of module 41. For nonempty E, the class map measured against any base section is an equivalence (Π P)/∼ ≃ Bool (parity_quotient_equiv). Thus the quotient is a two-element set. For empty E, the quotient is contractible and equal to Fin 1. The proof of transitivity uses the cocycle law parity(f,h) = parity(f,g) xor parity(g,h) (additivity of parities of counts). A second proof uses the book's Venn-diagram count Card(F12)+Card(F13)+Card(F23) = 2(…) (parity_venn_count, parity_venn_transitive, module 463). The proof's remark that the quotient has at most two classes is parity_quotient_at_most_two. Litmus: for E = Fin 1, the constant sections at 0 and 1 are in different classes. For E = Fin 2, they are in the same class.

μ_E : Hom(Σ_2^E, Σ_2) uses the decision finite_inhabited_decidable whether E is inhabited. Here Σ_2^E = power_group of module 407. If E is nonempty, Bμ_E(P) = (Π P)/∼. Its pointing is Fin 2 ≃ (E → Fin 2)/∼, which sends 0 to the class of the constant section at 0 (sign_mu_point_zero). The formalization identifies {±1} with Fin 2 by +1 = 0 and −1 = 1. If E is empty, Bμ_E is constant at sh with refl pointing. Then BΣ_2^E is contractible, and this is the unique homomorphism (sign_mu_empty_unique).

sign_mu_usym_product: the sign of USym μ_E(g) is the product of the signs of the components g(e) = happly g e. This is the map of power_group_usym_equiv. The lemma sign_mu_product states it for s : E → {±1} through USym(Σ_2^E) ≃ {±1}^E. This step uses function extensionality and the footnote identification. The product over a finite set is (−1)^(number of −1 values). The lemmas sign_product_fin_zero/_fin_succ show that it is the iterated product on Fin n. The footnote (empty product +1) is sign_product_empty, and the E-empty case covers it.

E(A) is KSubsets A 2 (module 178). P(e) is the carrier of e as a point of BΣ_2. A finite set is given as (A, isSet A, IsFinite A). Litmus: Fin 3 has 8 local orderings, and its sign orderings form a two-element set.

Bsgn(A) ≔ Bμ_{E(A)}(P) for A : BΣ_n. Its pointing is the pointing of Bμ, followed by Bμ applied to an identification of the constant family with P. This identification sends 0 ↦ min and 1 ↦ max in each two-element subset {i < j} of Fin n (order fin_lt, 0 = inr star). The definition is made for every n, as printed. For n = 0, 1, there are no two-element subsets, and Bsgn is constant at the standard two-element set (bsgn_small_constant). That is, sgn is trivial there (the book only uses n ≥ 2). For n ≥ 2, Bsgn(A) is identified with the set of sign orderings of A (bsgn_quotient_path). Also, USym sgn is the parity of the disagreement of the transported standard local ordering with itself (usgn_sign_parity).

For n ≥ 2, Σ_{A:BΣ_n} Bsgn(A), pointed at (n, Bsgn_pt(pt_2)) with pt_2 = 0 ∈ Fin 2, is a pointed connected groupoid. Then A_n = alternating_group_printed. Correction: for n = 0, 1, this type is not connected, because Bsgn is constant at a two-element set (alternating_shapes_small_not_connected). Thus the printed definition is not a group. The corrected A_n for all n is the automorphism group (component) of the designated shape. For n ≥ 2, it is equal to the printed one (alternating_group_printed_path). The gloss is formalized. The designated shape carries the class of the standard local ordering (alternating_point_standard). The symmetries of A_n are the even permutations (alternating_usym_even). Litmus: A_3 has 3 symmetries.

C_3 = cyclic_group_fin 2 (Aut_Cyc(Fin 3, s)), and A_3 = alternating_group_printed 1. The maps ψ, ψ' : C_3 → A_3 send a 3-cycle (X, t) to X with the sign ordering of a local ordering. In each pair {x, t x}, this local ordering chooses the target t x (ψ) or the source x (ψ'). The two maps are isomorphisms, because their loop maps are bijections. The reason is that a permutation of Fin 3 commutes with s iff it is even (c3_commutes_iff_even). The proof uses the loops criterion of module 185. The two isomorphisms A_3 → C_3 are their inverses (through group_path_iso_equiv). They differ, because ψ(s) and ψ'(s) act on 0 ∈ Fin 3 by 1 and 2.

Let A be a finite set (FiniteSets) with n = Card A. Then A is a point of BΣ_n, and σ is the loop ua(σ). The definition permutation_sign_at matches on n. For n = 0, 1, the sign is +1. Otherwise, it is two_loop_sign of ap Bsgn of the loop. This is −1 exactly when the transport swaps the two elements of Bsgn(A) (two_loop_moves). Even means sign +1 (IsEvenPermutation). The following prose gives the concrete sgn^A : Hom(Aut(A), Σ_2) (group.tex:1663, sign_aut_hom). It induces this sign on symmetries: sign_aut_usym_permutation_sign_finite (module 462).

(1) transposition_sign: every transposition (a b), a ≠ b, of a finite set has sign −1. By transport invariance, the proof reduces to (i j) on Fin n. This transposition is conjugate to (0 1). The disagreement of (0 1) with the standard local ordering is the single inversion (usgn_swap01). (2) cycle_sign: a k-cycle (a_1 … a_k) = cycle_notation_equiv (module 174) has sign (−1)^(k−1), with k − 1 = length rest. The proof uses xca:perm-prod-transpositions (cycle_transposition_product) and multiplicativity. (3) identity_word_even: if id equals the composite of a word of transpositions (module 176), then the word has even length.
If σ equals the composites of two words of transpositions, then their lengths have the same parity (sign_defined_parity). Also, sgn(σ) = (−1)^length for each word (permutation_sign_word).

Inversions n σ are the ordered pairs (i, j) with i < j and σ(j) < σ(i) in the standard order of Fin n. The number of these pairs is inv(σ), and sgn(σ) = (−1)^inv(σ) (permutation_sign_at_inversions). This holds for every n. For n ≥ 2, it also holds for USym sgn. The proof identifies the disagreement set of σ·ω₀ and ω₀ with the inversions through E(Fin n) ≃ ordered pairs. The parenthetical claim about other totally ordered sets is not formalized (see claims). Litmus: inversion_number 3 τ = 1 by refl, and sgn τ = −1 for τ = (0 1) in Σ_3.

Formalized: the number of inversions depends on the linear order. A relabeling of Fin 3 by (1 2) changes (0 2), with 3 inversions, into (0 1), with 1 inversion. But the sign and the parity of the number of inversions do not depend on the order (sign_independent_of_ordering, inversion_parity_independent). Composition of permutations preserves the parity of crossings (crossings_parity_compose). In the figure, (1 2)(1 2) = id has 1 + 1 crossings and then 0 crossings. The remarks on what the two pictures make visible and on pulling strings taut are informal.

even_permutations_half: for n ≥ 2, the number c of even permutations of Fin n satisfies c + c = n!. Here n! comes from xca:factorial (fin_automorphisms_equiv of module 175). That is, there are n!/2 even permutations. Multiplication by (0 1) exchanges even and odd permutations. For n = 3, c = 3 (even_permutations_three).

Bicycles is the displayed formula with the printed nesting: Σ (X : SetTypes) Σ (a : X ≃ X) Σ (b : X ≃ X) (Mere X × Π x x', Mere (Σ ℓ, x' = ⟦ℓ⟧(x))). Here ∃ is Mere of Σ, and words are ℓ : List (Sum Int Int). The power aⁿ is the integer power permutation_power (Int has neg n = −(n+1)). The meaning ⟦ℓ⟧ of group.tex 1870–1877 (bicycle_meaning, an Equiv X X) is defined by list induction on its underlying map. Thus the printed clauses ⟦ε⟧ = id, ⟦inl n ℓ⟧ = aⁿ∘⟦ℓ⟧ and ⟦inr n ℓ⟧ = bⁿ∘⟦ℓ⟧ hold by definition for maps. They also hold as identifications of equivalences (bicycle_meaning_nil/cons_left/cons_right). The reading as a 'subtype of Σ_{X:U}(X→X)×(X→X)' is covered by self_map_pairs_paths_equiv and bicycle_isomorphism_map_embedding (module 471).

The forward claim 'bicycles are the connected coverings over S¹ ∨ S¹' is proved for every FigureEightSignature. This is the HIT with base and two loops described in the remark. It is a signature with dependent induction and a propositional computation law, like CircleSignature in chapter 3. No HIT exists in the pinned Narya, and the formalization constructs no inhabitant here. The result is ConnectedCoverings(S¹∨S¹) ≃ Bicyc as a BookEquiv. The bicycle is the fiber over base, with the transports along loop₁ and loop₂. The formalization also proves the universal property (S¹∨S¹ → A) ≃ Σ_{a}(a = a)×(a = a). It also proves that set families are equivalent to sets with two permutations. The generalization to S-fold cycles over BF_S and the groupoid property of BF_S are forward references or historical (informal). The same holds for the picture and the footnote on bicyclic groups.

The formalization proves that both standard bicycles with the printed a, b are bicycles. The first is Z ⊔ Z = Sum Int Int, with a(inl n) = inl(n+1), written int_add n 1. The second is Fin 8 with k = inl^k(inr ⋆), given by tables of the printed mod-8 formulas. Bicyc is a groupoid (bicycles_groupoid, through bicycle_paths_equiv). D∞ and Q₈ are automorphism_group Bicycles bicycles_groupoid of these bicycles. Litmus: for the printed a, b of the quaternion bicycle, a⁴ = b⁴ = id, a² = b² (k ↦ k+4) ≠ id, bab⁻¹ = a⁻¹ and aba = b. Also, USym Q₈ ≃ Fin 8 and |Q₈| = 8, and USym D∞ ≃ Z ⊔ Z. The figure fig:quaternion-bicycle draws the arrows k → a(k) of the printed formula in the colour of b, and the arrows of b in the colour of a. We follow the formula. The footnote is a forward reference (informal).

Take bicycles B, B' and x₀. The map ev_{x₀}(e) = e(x₀) is injective in the sense of def:injection (IsEmbedding: propositional book fibers). It is also path-reflecting. Here bicycle_path_evaluate gives the underlying equivalence of e under bicycle_paths_equiv. This equivalence is transport along the path of sets (bicycle_path_evaluate_transport, by refl). The proof follows the book. List induction gives e⟦ℓ⟧ = ⟦ℓ⟧'e (bicycle_meaning_intertwine), and then connectivity completes the proof (bicycle_commuting_maps_agree).
IsNormalBicycle B ≔ Π (x : X), BookIsEquiv (Id Bicycles B B) X (bicycle_evaluation B x), with bicycle_evaluation B x p = p(x). It is a proposition.

If ev_x is a BookIsEquiv for some x, then ev_y is a BookIsEquiv for every y. The symmetry e_z ∘ e_y⁻¹ sends y to z, with e_w = ev_x⁻¹(w) and composition as isomorphisms. Thus ev_y is surjective. It is injective by lem:evisinj-bicycle (lem:inj+surj). The variant normal_bicycle_from_point_surjective (merely surjective at one point) is the one used for D∞ and Q₈.

For a normal bicycle, cbid x x' is the center of the contractible book fiber of ev_x over x'. Thus x' = cbid x x' (x). The lemma bicycle_cbid_unique says that every symmetry that sends x to x' equals it. The lemma normal_bicycle_unique_symmetry states the preceding sentence of the text. That sentence says that a unique permutation commutes with a, b and maps x to x'.

H_x ≔ {ℓ | ⟦ℓ⟧(x) = x} is bicycle_stabilizer B x : Subtypes (List (Sum Int Int)) (Sub of def:subtype). The exercise is the equivalence of propositions IsNormalBicycle B ≃ Π x y, H_x = H_y (equality in Sub). For H_x = H'_y, the ⇐ direction constructs an isomorphism of bicycles that sends x to y (bicycle_iso_from_point). This is the bicycle analogue of lem:IdCycle. Unique choice gives f(⟦ℓ⟧x) ≔ ⟦ℓ⟧'y.

First part as printed: commuting bicycles (a(b x) = b(a x) for all x) are normal. Second part refuted: the map ((X,t),(Y,u)) ↦ (X×Y, t×id, id×u) lands in the commuting bicycles, but it is not onto them. The commuting bicycle (Bool, not, not) is not in its image (cycle_product_not_onto_commuting). Corrected statement, proved: the map is an equivalence Cyc × Cyc ≃ SplitCommutingBicycles. These are the commuting bicycles with aⁿbᵐz = z ⇒ aⁿz = z. The inverse takes the orbit sets Z/⟨b⟩ and Z/⟨a⟩ with the induced permutations. The bicycle (Bool, not, not) is not split. Footnote: the picture shows a 4-element commuting bicycle. From the TikZ, a flips the second coordinate and b flips the first coordinate. For this bicycle, Aut_Bicyc = C₂ × C₂ (klein_bicycle_automorphism_path). The proof uses Aut_Bicyc(product bicycle) = product of the cyclic automorphism groups. The last step, from C₂ = Σ₂ to the Klein four-group Σ₂ × Σ₂, is xca:CG2isSG2 (another part).

The standing assumption of the preceding text is a normal bicycle with x₀. Under this assumption, the surjection ⟦-⟧(x₀) induces a relation (bicycle_word_relation). This relation relates ℓ, ℓ' iff ⟦ℓ⟧ = ⟦ℓ'⟧ as equivalences X ≃ X. This is an equivalence of propositions (Id X ⟦ℓ⟧x₀ ⟦ℓ'⟧x₀) ≃ (Id (X ≃ X) ⟦ℓ⟧ ⟦ℓ'⟧).

The formalization proves all displayed equalities for a normal bicycle and words ℓ, ℓ' (ℓ'ℓ = append ℓ' ℓ). Symmetries commute with ⟦ℓ⟧. Also, cbid x x' = cbid ⟦ℓ⟧x ⟦ℓ⟧x', and ⟦ℓ'⟧⟦ℓ⟧ = ⟦ℓ'ℓ⟧ (pointwise). Both two-step calculations are proved as identifications in Id Bicyc B B. There, the book's composite g ∘ f of symmetries is written concat f g. The 'punchline' sentence is informal.

The statements hold for every normal bicycle and base point x₀. T = cbid(ax₀, x₀) = cbid(x₀, a⁻¹x₀), and R = cbid(bx₀, x₀) = cbid(x₀, b⁻¹x₀). Also, T(⟦ℓ⟧x₀) = ⟦ℓ inl(−1)⟧x₀ and R(⟦ℓ⟧x₀) = ⟦ℓ inr(−1)⟧x₀, with the middle cbid expressions. Also, a(T⁻²R x₀) = T⁻²RT⁻¹x₀, with T⁻¹ the inverse symmetry and composites as functions. For the infinite dihedral bicycle, R(aⁿx₀) = aⁿbx₀ for every x₀. At x₀ = inl 0, T = σ⁺₋₁ (downward translation) and R = σ⁻₀ (half turn). The frieze pictures and the words 'geometric symmetries' are informal. The references to fig:plus-minus-one and ch:euclidean are also informal.

Let x₀ = inl 0, as in fig:first-frieze-bicycle. Take the permutations that underlie the symmetries T and R. Then (X, T, R) is a bicycle. It is identified with (X, a, b) through e(inl n) = inl(−n) and e(inr n) = inr n (ea = Te, eb = Re).

The pictured bicycles are read off the TikZ. The hexagon is on Fin 6, with a = (0 1)(2 3)(4 5) and b = (1 2)(3 4)(5 0). The prism is on Fin 3 ⊔ Fin 3, with a(x_k) = x_{k−1}, a(y_k) = y_{k+1} and b(x_k) = y_k. Both are identified with Cayley bicycles of Σ₃, for (0 1), (1 2) and for (0 1 2), (1 2), respectively. For generating g, h, G = Aut_Bicyc(Cay(G; g, h)) (cayley_bicycle_group_path). This gives Aut(hexagon) = Σ₃ = Aut(prism) as identifications of groups and as GroupIso. Also formalized: both bicycles are normal, and they lie in different components (hexagon_prism_different_components).

U^{>0}_* = Σ(A:U) A × isconn(A) is the record PointedConnectedType (carrier, point, connected), with the components in the printed order. The type of ∞-groups is a wrapped copy of it, with the constructor mk_infty_group and the destructor infty_group_B (the book's clf). As for Group (module 400), the wrapper is a one-field record instead of the data type Copy of module 16. Thus mk_infty_group (infty_group_B G) ≡ G and infty_group_B (mk_infty_group X) ≡ X hold judgmentally. That is, infty_group_classifying_equiv is refl in both directions.

The synonymy of ∞-groups and pointed connected types (wrapped with mkgroup) is the equivalence infty_group_classifying_equiv : InftyGroup ≃ PointedConnectedType. Both directions hold by refl. The analogue for groups is group_classifying_equiv. The omission of the propositional component, (A, a) for (A, a, !), is a notational convention without separate content.
infty_BG G : Pointed is the underlying pointed type (carrier, point) of the classifying pointed connected type. Its base point infty_shape G is the designated shape.

For any type A and a : A, infty_automorphism_group A a = mk_infty_group (A_(a), (a, |refl|), connectedness of the component). Here A_(a) = NativeComponent A a = Σ(x:A) ‖a = x‖. There is no groupoid hypothesis on A.

First paragraph: for a set S, the component U_(S) is a groupoid (universe_set_component_groupoid). The proof uses (X = Y) ≃ (X ≃ Y) for sets. Thus Aut_U(S) is an ordinary group (universe_set_automorphism_group). Its ∞-group is literally infty_automorphism_group Type S. The formalization completes the example with a proof that U itself is not a groupoid (universe_not_groupoid). This proof uses the central loop of the constructed circle and loop ≠ refl. Thus 'the component can be a groupoid although A is not' is a theorem (universe_component_groupoid_not_universe). Second paragraph: the inclusion U^{=1}_* ↪ U^{>0}_* induces group_to_infty_group : Group → InftyGroup. Its action on identity types is an equivalence (group_infty_paths_equiv). Therefore it is an embedding in the book's sense, with proposition-valued fibers (group_to_infty_group_embedding). Litmus: the symmetries of Aut_U(A) are the self-equivalences of A (infty_universe_automorphisms_equiv).

Hom(G, H) of ∞-groups is a wrapped copy of BG →* BH in the book's pointing orientation (BookPointedMap, pt_BH = f(pt_BG)). Again, it is a one-field record (judgmental eta) instead of Copy. The classifying map Bf is infty_hom_B.

GSet G is BG÷ → SetTypes. X(p) and p ·_X a are transport in z ↦ X z .fst (gset_act). For g : USym G, the action on X(sh_G) is gset_usym_act. With the chapter-4 product g·h = concat h g, it is a left action: (g·h)·a = g·(h·a) and e·a = a (gset_act_mul, gset_act_unit). These laws are typal identifications, because J has only a typal β-rule. The formalization also gives X(p) as an equivalence (gset_act_equiv). The map of this equivalence is gset_act.
triv_G S is the constant family z ↦ S. Its action is the identity up to the typal transport law in a constant family (gset_trivial_act).

gset_coverings_equiv : GSet G ≃ Coverings(BG) is the inverse of the chapter-3 equivalence coverings_setfamilies_equiv. Its map sends X to the first projection Σ_{z:BG} X(z) → BG, and refl checks both components. The inverse sends a covering to its fiber family. The core declaration action_type_projection_covering records that this projection is a covering.

Core: P_G(z) ≔ (sh_G = z) and P_y(z) ≔ (y = z) (gset_paths). Definitionally, P_G(sh_G) ≡ USym G and the action is p · q ≡ concat q p (the book's p q). gset_paths_map_equiv_value: P_- applied to q : y = y' is the family of equivalences that sends p : y = z to p q⁻¹ = concat q⁻¹ p (typal, core gset_paths_transport). principal_gset_universal_cover: P_G and every P_y are literally the family path_cover_family of def:universalcover (refl). lem:BGbytorsor and the G-torsors of the footnote are core (Torsors, bg_torsors_equiv).

Core: Ad_G(z) ≔ (z = z) with Ad_G(p)(q) = p q p⁻¹ (adjoint_gset_act, typal). In concatenation order, this is concat p⁻¹ (concat q p). Compare the contrasting P_G(p)(q) = p q (gset_paths_act, refl). adjoint_free_loops_equiv : Σ_{z:BG} Ad_G(z) ≃ (S¹ → BG) holds for every CircleSignature C (lem:freeloopspace). Its inverse is f ↦ (f(base), ap_f(loop)), so the first projection is evaluation at base (refl). The map evaluated at base is fst (typal, circle_rec_beta). The remark that Ad_G makes sense for ∞-groups is not formalized, because the formalization defines only groups.

group_hom_pair_gset : GSet (H × G) sends (x, y) to Hom(mkgroup(BH÷, x), mkgroup(BG÷, y)). It uses group_at of module 437, and these are sets by lem:hom-is-set. It uses B(H × G) ≡ BH × BG. group_hom_gset H G (y) ≔ Hom(H, G)(sh_H, y) is literally the restriction along the inclusion G → H × G (refl). Its underlying set is Hom(H, G) (refl, record eta). group_hom_pair_unfold: Hom(H,G)(x,y) ≃ Σ_{f : BH÷ → BG÷} (y = f(x)). Here the record Copy_mkgroup is around the pointed map, and both round trips are refl.

Let Z = circle_group C for any CircleSignature C. Then adjoint_hom_z_path : Ad_G = Hom(Z, G) in GSet G. The proof builds it from the equivalences Hom(Z, mkgroup(BG÷, y)) ≃ (y = y), f ↦ Ω(Bf)(loop) (ex:Zinitial, circle_group_hom_ev of module 435). Module 435 contains the contract-away hint of the book. Transport along this identification is f ↦ f(loop) (typal). adjoint_hom_integer_path is the instance Z = integer_group.
Hom_G(X,Y) ≔ Π_{z:BG} (X(z) → Y(z)), as printed. It is a set (gset_hom_set). The formalization adds identity, composition (g ∘ f, f first) and extensionality for later use.

gset_hom_totalization_equiv : Hom_G(X,Y) ≃ Σ_{f : Tot(X) → Tot(Y)} (fst = fst ∘ f). As in the book, this uses the identification of functions Tot(X) → BG. The map sends h to its totalization with reflexivity (refl check). It is the G-set instance of fiberwise_maps_over_equiv for families over any type (choice, lem:contract-away, currying).

Core (module 500): gset_hom_natural states f_w(g ·_X x) = g ·_Y f_z(x) for g : z = w (the commuting square). gset_hom_equivariant is its restriction to USym G. For Y = triv_G Prop, gsubset_invariant identifies P_w(g · x) with P_z(x) in Prop, and gsubset_invariant_iff gives the two implications. The trivial action is typal (gset_trivial_act).

Core: Sub_G(X) ≔ Hom_G(X, triv_G Prop). This is definitionally Π_{z:BG} Sub(X(z)) (gsubsets_unfold, refl), and it is a set (gsubsets_set). X_P(z) ≔ Σ_{x:X(z)} P(z)(x) (gsubset_gset). Footnote ft:SubTotX: gsubsets_total_equiv : Sub_G(X) ≃ (Tot(X) → Prop) by uncurrying (curry_equiv). The map is uncurrying (refl check).

gsubsets_closed_equiv : Sub_G(X) ≃ Σ_{Q : Sub(X(sh_G))} Π_x (Q(x) → Π_{g:USym G} Q(g · x)). The first component of the map is evaluation at sh_G (refl). The closure proof comes from rem:map-of-Gsets. The inverse sends Q to (z, x) ↦ Π_{p : z = sh_G} Q(p · x). The round trips use proposition extensionality and the connectedness of BG.

Chapter-4 module 436 proves this (pointed_maps_into_component, which that module uses for xca:BGtotype). ptd_conn_to_comp_equiv restates it for pointed types (A,a), (B,b) with A connected: ((A,a) →* (B,b)) ≃ ((A,a) →* (B_(b),(b,!))), with BookPointedMap (b = f(a)). The map is (f,p) ↦ (x ↦ (f(x),!), component path over p). This agrees with the commented hint of the book. The values, the pointing path and the inverse round trip are refl checks.

gset_action_equiv : GSet G ≃ Σ_{S:Set} Hom(G, Σ_S) has the map X ↦ (X(sh_G), gset_to_action G X) and the inverse action_to_gset. The round trip on GSet is refl. It agrees with the chain of the book up to the propositional component witnesses. The chain is: contract away, pointed maps, xca:ptd-conn-to-comp, and Hom ≡ pointed maps into Set_(S). The formalization of this chain is gset_action_composite_equiv. gset_to_action_usym_act: g acts through the homomorphism as g ·_X - (typal). action_to_gset_usym_act: the pointing path of f identifies the underlying set of the delooped G-set with S, and the action is f(g). The word 'delooping' in the footnote is a forward reference (sec:delooping).

An action of G on a set S is GroupHom G (permutation_group S), which is literally Hom(G, Σ_S). The two directions of the identification with G-sets (rem:GSet=SetHomG) are gset_to_action and action_to_gset. One round trip is refl.

The formalization reads 'identical' as an identification in GSet G: IsAbelian G ⇔ Ad_G = triv_G(USym G). (⇒) The identity of USym G is a fixed point of z ↦ (Ad_G(z) → USym G), because conjugation is trivial. So it extends to an invariant family (gset_fixed_point_extension, through weakly constant maps into sets). By connectedness, this family consists of equivalences. (⇐) The equivariance of the transport makes g h g⁻¹ = h. Litmus: Ad ≠ triv for Σ_3.

adjoint_principal_iff_trivial: G = TG (the trivial group of the book, module 506) iff Ad_G = P_G in GSet G. The proof goes through IsTrivialGroup (BG contractible). Contractible path types give the fiberwise equivalences. Conversely, transport of the invariant section z ↦ refl_z of Ad_G gives a contraction z ↦ (sh_G = z) of BG. Litmus: Ad = P for the unit group, and Ad ≠ P for Σ_3.

Core: IsFiniteGSet G X ≔ IsFinite(X(sh_G)) and Card(X) ≔ Card(X(sh_G)). Footnote: gset_finite_at_iff states that, for each z : BG, X(sh_G) is finite iff X(z) is finite. gset_finite_everywhere_iff gives the equivalence with the statement that all X(z) are finite. The same results hold for n-element sets ‖(Fin n,!) = X(z)‖ (as in BookFiniteSetsAt). They come from the general gset_set_property_at_iff for propositional properties of sets and from the connectedness of BG.
istrans(X) ≔ ∃_{x:X(sh)} Π_{y:X(sh)} ∃_{g:USym G} (x = g·y), literally, with Mere for ∃. It is a proposition.

The formalization proves that each reformulation is logically equivalent to IsTransitive. First: ∃x such that - · x : USym G → X(sh_G) is surjective (Surjective, with the book's fibers y = g · x). Second: eq:Gset-trans-gen at every z : BG (GSetTransitiveAt at sh_G is literally IsTransitive, refl). Third: X(sh_G) is merely inhabited and ∀x y ∃g (x = g · y). 'The empty G-set is not transitive': gset_empty_not_transitive for triv_G ∅ (through gset_transitive_nonempty).

X is transitive iff the domain Tot(X) = Σ_{z:BG} X(z) of the associated covering fst : Tot(X) → BG is connected. This map is a covering by action_type_projection_covering. As in the book, the proof reduces to the base point by the connectedness of BG.

For transitive X, ev_x : Hom_G(X,Y) → Y(z), f ↦ f_z(x), is an injection (all fibers are propositions, IsEmbedding). As in the book, the proof transports the equation f_z(x) = f'_z(x) along merely existing identifications (z,x) = (w,x') in Tot(X).

S¹ ∨ S¹ is a parameter CircleWedgeSignature (base, two loops, dependent induction with a typal computation law). Its carrier is a groupoid for every such signature (circle_wedge_carrier_groupoid, module 596). The reason is that a CircleWedgeSignature is a free-group signature on Bool (def:bfree, chapter 8). By the encode-decode method of chapter 8, the carrier of such a signature is a groupoid (free_signature_groupoid). So the results hold without hypothesis (*_unconditional, for example wedge_gset_not_normal_unconditional). The results are also not vacuous. constructed_circle_wedge_signature (no HITs) has the carrier of the constructed S¹ ∨ S¹ of chapter 8, and mkgroup(S¹ ∨ S¹) = F_2 (constructed_circle_wedge_group_path). Every chapter-8 wedge signature of two circles is a groupoid. It is pointed-equal to the wedge of any CircleWedgeSignature (chapter8_circle_wedge_groupoid, chapter8_circle_wedge_pointed_path). X (wedge_gset) sends base to Fin 3, loop₁ to s = (0 1 2) and loop₂ to t = (0 1). This is the graph of the figures after the relabelling n1 ↦ 2, n2 ↦ 0, n3 ↦ 1, so x = n2 = 0. X(base) ≃ Fin 3 holds only through the computation law (wedge_identify). X = X is contractible. For every x, ev_x is injective but not surjective. X is not normal.

IsNormalGSet G X ≔ every ev_x : (X = X) → X(z), e ↦ e_z(x), is a BookIsEquiv. Here e_z(x) is the transport along e at z. The book has the standing hypothesis that X is transitive. The formalization keeps it as a separate hypothesis where it is necessary, and does not build it into the predicate.

normal_eval_equiv_everywhere: if ev_x : (X = X) → X(z) is a (book) equivalence for one z and x : X(z), then IsNormalGSet G X holds. That is, ev at every pair is an equivalence. Transitivity is not necessary. For x' = ev_x(e), ev_{x'} = ev_x ∘ (e · -). The proof reaches the other fibers by a mere path z = w and transport in Tot(X). normal_action_equiv is the setting of the book (X transitive).

Core: an action of G in A is X : BG → A, which acts on X(sh_G). An action on a : A is ActionOnElement G A a ≔ BG →* (A_(a),(a,!)). When A is a groupoid, this is literally Hom(G, Aut_A(a)) (action_on_element_group_hom_equiv). The displayed equivalence of the subsequent text is action_in_type_equiv : (BG → A) ≃ Σ_{a:A} ActionOnElement G A a for every type A. Its map is X ↦ (X(sh_G), z ↦ (X(z),!)) (refl check). action_in_type_group_equiv gives Σ_a Hom(G, Aut_A(a)) for groupoids A (compare bg_to_type_one_four, module 436).
The standard action is id : BG → BG as an action in A ≔ BG. Its object is sh_G by definition.

Let S be a 2-element set (BΣ_2 ≡ 2-element sets). Then T_S ≔ Σ_{X:Set} (S → X → X). The point is (1 ⊔ S, f) with f_s(inl 0) = inr s, f_s(inr s) = inr(swap s) and f_s(inr swap s) = inl 0. Here swap s is the other element, which comes from contractibility. The case split uses the decidable equality of S, and the three equations hold typally. G(S) ≔ Aut_{T_S}(1 ⊔ S, f) gives s2_acts_on_c3 : BΣ_2 → Group. G(Fin 2) = C_3 = Aut_Cyc(Fin 3, s) (s2c3_group_c3_path). On classifying types, the map is (X, f) ↦ (X, f_yes). It goes through the subtype where f_yes is a cyclic permutation and f_no = f_yes ∘ f_yes (Σ T Q ≃ Cycles). Also, (1 ⊔ Fin 2, f_yes) = (Fin 3, s) by inl 0 ↦ 0, yes ↦ 1, no ↦ 2. The footnote picture is informal.

The action of ex:S2-acts-on-C3 is a pointed map b : BΣ_2 → BAut(C_3) ≡ Group_(C_3). It sends S to (G(S), ‖C_3 = G(S)‖) and is pointed by G(Fin 2) = C_3 (s2c3_group_c3_path). This map is an equivalence (s2_aut_c3_map_equiv). It gives the isomorphism s2_aut_c3_iso and the identification s2_aut_c3_path : Σ_2 = Aut(C_3) = group_aut (cyclic_group_fin two). Its classifying map is literally S ↦ G(S) on first components (s2_aut_c3_classifying, refl). Proof: on loops, b is ap_G. It is injective because the Σ_2-set S ↦ USym G(S) maps equivariantly to 1 ⊔ S (evaluation at inl 0). This map sends the symmetry u₀ given by f_yes to inr yes. It is surjective because G(Fin 2) = G(Fin 2) injects into Fin 2 (module 573). That is, the image gen^k, k ∈ {1,2}, of the generator determines an automorphism of C_3, through abstract isomorphisms (chapter 7, module 709). Then connected_map_equiv_from_loops applies. Litmus: Aut(C_3) ≃ Fin 2 on symmetries (aut_c3_usym_fin_two), and swap acts nontrivially (s2c3_swap_acts_nontrivially).

The standard Σ_n-set (core standard_symmetric_gset, z ↦ z.fst) is literally the composite of the standard action id_{BΣ_n} with the projection BΣ_n → Set (refl). Footnote: it is transitive for n > 0, because the transposition (0 y) sends y to 0. It is not transitive for n = 0 (empty). decidable_subsets_gset n ≔ z ↦ (z → Bool) composes further with S ↦ (S → Bool) : Set → Set. Its action satisfies (g · s)(g · x) = s(x) (typal), with a Σ_3 litmus.

Sub(G) is a record (gset, point, transitive) with the three components of the printed Σ_{X:BG→Set} X(sh_G) × istrans(X). subgroups_sigma_equiv identifies it with the literal Σ-type (both round trips are refl).
For transitive X, Σ_{z:BG} X(z) is connected (lem:conistrans) and a groupoid. This gives a pointed connected groupoid at (sh_G, x).
The underlying group of (X,pt) is mkgroup(Tot(X), (sh_G, pt)). Its classifying pointed type is that pair by definition.

Let C be any circle (Z = circle_group C) and let m = n+1. Then (R_m, 0) : Sub(Z) with R_m = power_circle_family C n. It is transitive because Tot(R_m) is connected. R_m(base) ≡ Fin m holds only through the circle β-identification, so 0 is power_bundle_zero. A symmetry p fixes 0 iff ‖Σ k, p = loop^{k·m}‖ (rmsub_picks_out). The proof uses p · 0 = R_m(loop)^{w(p)}(0) and the monodromy (Fin m, s). For m = 0, the subgroup is (R, 0) with R = circle_integer_family (sets by code_is_set). Then R(loop^k)(0) = k (rsub_power_act), and p fixes 0 iff p = refl (rsub_picks_out). The remarks that relate this to dg_m / α_m and to R as universal covering are motivation. The same is true for the footnote 'any element of Fin m would do'. They are not formalized separately.

Sub(G) is a set. As in the book, ((X,pt) = (X',pt')) is equivalent to the fiber of ev_pt : (X = X') → X'(sh_G) at pt' (pointed_gset_path_fiber_equiv). This fiber has the native orientation ev(e) = pt'. It is a proposition, because ev_pt is injective for transitive X. The transitivity component is a proposition.

Let n = m+1. The Σ_n-set X(A, !) ≔ A (core standard_symmetric_gset) is transitive. The reason is that its action type is the type of pointed (m+1)-element sets, which is equivalent to the connected FinSet_m (xca:n-is-ptd-n+1). So (X, k) : Sub(Σ_n) for every k : Fin n. The symmetries picked out are the π with π·k = k (lem:E-preserves-symms). The underlying group of (X, k) is identified with Σ_{n−1} (fixed_point_subgroup_group_path). This is a pointed equivalence through xca:n-is-ptd-n+1 and Fin(m+1) ∖ {k} ≃ Fin m. The footnote states that the choice of k matters for the symmetries picked out. It is not formalized separately.

FinSet_n ≃ Σ_{S:FinSet_{n+1}} S by A ↦ (A ⊔ 1, inr ★). The inverse is (S, s) ↦ S ∖ {s}, which is n-element by Fin(n+1) ∖ {a} ≃ Fin n. As the hint says, the decidability of S comes from finiteness (xca:finsets-decidable).

Let A be any type with decidable equality. Then a ↦ (A ∖ {a}, ua(A ≃ (A ∖ {a}) + 1)) is a BookEquiv A ≃ Σ_{B:U} (A = B + 1). Here A ∖ {a} is Without A a of chapter 2. The inverse is (B, p) ↦ p⁻¹(inr ★). The hypothesis that A is a set is not necessary, because decidable equality is sufficient.

C_6 = cyclic_group_fin 5 and F(X,t) = X/2 = ModQuotient 1 (the quotient by the orbit relation of t²). π · [k] = [π(k)] (c6half_act_class). π picks out [0] iff π(0) is even, that is, iff π is an even power of s by cor:id-m-cycle. The formal statement uses g ↦ g(0), not explicit powers. Footnote: the same holds for [1], and π·[0] = [1] iff π·[1] = [0] iff π(0) is odd. As in the book, ρ_2 : Cyc_3 → Cyc_6, thm:fiber-cdg and lem:sum-of-fibers give BC_3 ≃ Σ_{(X,t):BC_6} X/2. Here thm:fiber-cdg is root_order_fiber_equiv of module 145 (fibers over cycles of a given order). This equivalence sends the base point to ((Fin 6, s), [0]). Hence F is transitive (stated after the equivalence) and (F,[0]) : Sub(C_6). Its underlying group equals C_3 = cyclic_group_fin 2 (through cyclic_group 3). fig:C3inC6 is a picture (no claim beyond the above).
A subgroup (X,pt) is decidable if X(sh_G) has decidable equality (DecidableEquality of module 32).

ismono(i) ≔ USym i is an injection (IsEmbedding: propositional fibers) for i : GroupHom H G. Mono(G) ≔ Σ_H Σ_i ismono(i). A mono is proper if i is not an isomorphism. It is trivial if H is trivial, where IsTrivialGroup H ≔ BH contractible. trivial_group_iff_path shows that this is equivalent to H = TG ('H is the trivial group'). trivial_group_iff_usym_contractible shows that it is equivalent to USym H contractible.

i_n : Σ_n → Σ_{n+1} with Bi_n(A) = A ⊔ 1 (automorphism_group_map_hom of chapter 4 for S ↦ S ⊔ 1) is pointed by refl, literally. The reason is that standard_set (n+1) is (Fin n ⊔ 1, sum_set …) by definition. USym i_n(π) acts as π on Fin n and fixes the new element (inr ★, the 'last element' of the book). Hence USym i_n is injective. The margin picture for n = 2 is informal.

The printed exercise says i_3, but it means i_2 : Σ_2 → Σ_3. This also occurs in the preceding example. Take any m and any pointing path p : sh = sh of Bi_m (a permutation of Fin (m+1)). Then USym i^p(s) = p⁻¹·USym i_m(s)·p, and h ∈ im(USym i^p) iff h fixes p⁻¹·★. Here ★ = inr ★, the last element of the book. So for m = 2, the six pointing paths give the stabilizers of the three points, that is, the three subgroups {e, (a b)}, each twice. The general formula is the requested calculation. The formalization does not list the six cases one by one.

j : C_3 → Σ_3 is the forgetful homomorphism ((X,t),!) ↦ (X,!). j' = j ∘ α, with α the inversion automorphism (X,t) ↦ (X,t⁻¹). α is pointed by (Fin 3, s) = (Fin 3, s⁻¹) through the transposition (1 2). Both j and j' are monomorphisms (USym injective). USym j ≠ USym j' as functions (c3inv_usym_differ): j' sends the generator r_1 to a symmetry with value 2 at 0. But (C_3, j') = (C_3, j) in Mono(Σ_3) by the pointed equivalence Bα with Bj ∘ Bα = Bj' (c3inv_monos_path).

The first inclusion i_G (product_group_incl1 of chapter 4: Bi_G(z) = (z, sh_H), pointed by refl) is a monomorphism. USym i_G(g) = (g, refl_{sh_H}) (typal). The formalization uses both the argument of the book by injectivity and its footnote, and the proof goes through the footnote. The footnote states that the preimage of (z,t) contracts to the set t = sh_H, so Bi_G is a covering. The same is true for the second inclusion.

F(X,pt) = (mkgroup(Tot(X),(sh_G,pt)), mkgroup(fst)), with fst pointed by refl, is a BookIsEquiv. Its inverse is E(H,i) = (Bi÷⁻¹, (sh_H, Bi_pt)), exactly as in the proof. The monomorphism property of fst and the set-valuedness of Bi÷⁻¹ are cor:fib-vs-path (covering_group_mono, group_mono_covering).

The formalization proves this for every m (the case of the book is m = 2): F(X, inr ★) = (Σ_m, i_m) in Mono(Σ_{m+1}). Hence (X, inr ★) = E(Σ_m, i_m) in Sub(Σ_{m+1}). Here X(A,!) = A, and inr ★ is the added point (the '3' of the book). The book uses a pointwise route through xca:A-is-A-1+1 on the G-set side. Instead, the formalization makes the identification on the monomorphism side. BG of (X, inr ★) is the type of pointed (m+1)-element sets, ≃ FinSet_m (xca:n-is-ptd-n+1). Also, Bi_m(S ∖ s) = S by the splitting of xca:A-is-A-1+1. The pointing coherence is checked on permutations. E(Σ_2,i_2) ≡ (Bi_2⁻¹, (Fin 2, refl)) holds by definition. F(E(Σ_m,i_m)) = (Σ_m, i_m) is mono_subgroup_roundtrip. Here the book writes i_3 for i_2.

The formalization proves both round trips. E(F(X,pt)) = (X,pt) follows from the fiber equivalence fst⁻¹(z) ≃ X(z) (action_type_fiber_equiv). F(E(H,i)) = (H,i) follows from the sum of fibers BH ≃ Σ_z Bi⁻¹(z) (lem:sum-of-fibers), pointed by refl, together with a pointed homotopy Bi ∘ (that equivalence) ~ fst. pointed_over_path turns such data into an identification of pointed maps over BG (pointed-equivalence induction).
Mono(G) is a set. This property is transported from Sub(G) along the equivalence of lem:SubG=MonoG.

For every (X,pt), every (H,i) with (H,i) = F(X,pt) and every g : USym G: g ·_X pt = pt iff ∃h, g = USym i(h). As in the book, the formalization proves it for F(X,pt) itself and transports it along the given identification. The typal unit law of conjugation identifies USym of fst (pointed by refl) with the first projection.
Trivial: Tot(X) is contractible (the printed 'i.e.' form). Proper: X(sh_G) is not contractible.
This is a notational remark (H ⊆ G for a subgroup). It makes no mathematical claim.

F(P_{G'} ∘ proj_2, refl_{sh_G'}) = (G, i_1) in Mono(G × G'). As in the book, Tot(P_{G'} ∘ proj_2) ≃ BG (by contraction of Σ_{z'} (sh_G' = z')), pointed by refl, and fst = i_1 ∘ φ as pointed maps. pointed_over_path turns this into the identification of monomorphisms.

Let (X, pt) : Sub(G) with underlying group H. Then lagrange_construction : LagrangeChoice G X pt → Equiv (USym G) (X(sh_G) × USym H). Here LagrangeChoice is Π_{x} Σ_{g : USym G} (g · x = pt), as printed, and USym H ≡ ((sh_G, pt) = (sh_G, pt)) definitionally. The construction follows the implementation: [g] ≔ g · pt, lem:sum-of-fibers, fibers ≃ (sh_G, pt) = (sh_G, x), then postconcatenation with (g(x), !). xca:AC-in-TT is the definitional currying lagrange_choice_function_equiv. lagrange_equiv states it for any pointed G-set (transitivity is not used). The first component of L(f)(g) is g · pt by refl. The footnote says that the construction works for ∞-groups that act on types. It is not formalized (groups only).

For a choice f, L'(f) : Equiv (USym G) (Σ_{x : X(sh_G)} ((sh_G, x) = (sh_G, x))). It comes from preconcatenation with the inverse of (g(x), !), as in ft:lagrange-dep-sum. The formalization states it for any pointed G-set and for subgroups. lagrange_dep_sum_stabilizers reads (sh_G, x) = (sh_G, x) as USym(G_x).

Let G be a finite group and (X, pt) : Sub(G) with X a finite G-set. Then H is finite, because USym H ≃ {g | g · pt = pt}, which is a decidable subset of USym G. Also, Card(G) = Card(X) × Card(H). The choice function that con:lagrange needs exists merely (transitivity plus finite choice over X(sh_G), module 34). This is sufficient, because the goal is a proposition. The proof uses no classical principle.

con:lagrange (lagrange_construction, module 526) applies to Z = circle_group C and (R_m, 0) with underlying group H_m. It gives USym Z ≃ R_m(base) × USym H_m, hence ≃ Fin m × USym H_m (rmlag_fin_equiv). The first component of this equivalence is g ↦ g · 0. The premiss of con:lagrange is a choice of g with g · x = 0 for every x. The formalization constructs it explicitly, without a choice axiom. On (Z/m, s), s^{a−x} moves x to a. This is transported to (R_m(base), R_m(loop)) along the monodromy identification, and g = loop^z.

Let G = mkgroup(S¹ ∨ S¹), with a CircleWedgeSignature parameter. Module 596 proves that S¹ ∨ S¹ is a groupoid (see xca:not-normal). Let X be as printed (base ↦ Fin 3, loop₁ ↦ s, loop₂ ↦ (0 1)). Then wedge_choice_map : Π_{x : X(sh)} Σ_{g : USym G} (g · x = 0) is the choice map: e for 0, loop₁·loop₁ for 1 and loop₁ for 2. Here 0 ≔ E⁻¹(0), because X(sh) is Fin 3 only up to the computation law E. Lagrange's construction applies: wedge_lagrange_equiv_unconditional : USym G ≃ X(sh) × USym H for the subgroup (X, 0) with underlying group H. It is also stated as Fin 3 × USym H. It has no groupoid hypothesis, and the conditional versions of module 569 remain. The footnote (H is free, thm:nielsen-schreier) is a forward reference and is not formalized here.
X_hG ≔ Σ_{z:BG} X(z), X^hG ≔ Π_{z:BG} X(z) and X/G ≔ Σ_{P:Sub_G(X)} istrans(X_P), as printed. X/G is a set, and the G-subset of an orbit determines the orbit (orbit_path).

The untruncated equivalence ((z,x) = (w,y)) ≃ Σ_{g:z=w} (g·x = y) is action_type_path_equiv of the core (module 501). As the remark states, action_type_mere_path_equiv / action_type_mere_path_exists give the version for the propositional truncations: ‖(z,x) = (w,y)‖ ≃ ∃_{g:z=w} (g·x = y).
[u]_0 is the G-subset z ↦ (x ↦ ‖u = (z,x)‖) (orbit_subset). orbit_map packages it with the transitivity proof of lem:[]0-maps-to-X/G.

The underlying G-set z ↦ Σ_{x:X(z)} ‖u = (z,x)‖ of [u]_0 is transitive. Its action type is the component of u in X_hG (by reassociation, with refl round trips), and this component is connected. Hence [−]_0 : X_hG → X/G.

orbit_map_surjective: [-]_0 : X_hG → X/G is surjective. orbits_set_trunc_path_unique: the identity type (X/G, [-]_0) = (‖X_hG‖_0, |-|_0) in SetsWithMapFrom X_hG = Σ_{S:Set}(X_hG → S) is contractible. That is, the identification exists and is unique. orbits_set_trunc_unique states the equivalent factorization of the sentence after the lemma: the pairs of an equivalence ‖X_hG‖_0 ≃ X/G and a commuting triangle form a contractible type. As in the proof of the book, SetTrunc is the quotient of the repository by ‖x = y‖ (rem:set-trunc-as-quotient).

[x] = [y] ≃ ∃_{g:USym G} (g·x = y) (orbit_point_path_exists_equiv). [-] is surjective. For the quotient by ∃_g (g·x = y), the type of pairs (e : X(sh_G)/~ ≃ X/G, [-] = e ∘ class) is contractible (orbit_quotient_unique). This uses QuotientEquivalenceLifts of module 45, as for xca:map-induces-quotient. [x] is orbit_of_point of the core.

The formalization proves the chain Sub_G(X) ≡ Π_z (X(z) → Prop) ≃ (X_hG → Prop) ≃ (‖X_hG‖_0 → Prop) ≃ (X/G → Prop) ≡ Sub(X/G) step by step. Then it composes the steps (gsubsets_orbit_subsets_equiv). The inverse is precomposition with [-]_0 by definition (gsubsets_orbit_subsets_inverse). The proof of currying is local (gsubsets_total_equiv is not exported).
BookIsContr (X/G) ≃ IsTransitive G X (both are propositions). The proof uses the surjectivity of [-]_0, [u]_0 = [v]_0 ⇔ ‖u = v‖ and lem:conistrans.

The formalization shows that each listed proposition is equivalent to [x] =_{X/G} [y]. The first is [x](sh_G) = [y](sh_G) as maps X(sh_G) → Prop. The others are ∃_g (g·x = y), ‖(sh_G,x) = (sh_G,y)‖, [x](sh_G,y) and [y](sh_G,x). Here [x](sh_G,y) is definitionally ‖(sh_G,x) = (sh_G,y)‖. orbit_relation_induced identifies the relation ∃_g (g·x = y) with the relation that the surjection [-] induces (x ~ y iff ‖[x] = [y]‖, module 45). It does this as predicates X(sh_G) → X(sh_G) → Prop.
